statement: Sam throws a ball at a basket until one goes in, but he stops after 3 throws anyway. Each throw goes in or misses. In how many different ways can his throws go?

choices.misconception: I only looked at the first throw: in or miss.
I only counted the ways that end with the ball going in and forgot that all 3 throws could miss.
I counted 2 ways for each of the 3 throws and added them, 2 + 2 + 2.
I thought Sam always throws 3 times, so I counted every way 3 throws can go.

hints: Can Sam stop after just one throw?
Draw a tree. Each throw has two branches, in or miss. A branch that goes in stops there. Only a miss carries on, and the tree stops after 3 throws.
In stops at once. Miss then in stops after two throws. After two misses, the third throw can go in or miss, and both end the turn. Count the branch ends.

solutions.reliable: Write I for in and M for a miss. If the first throw goes in, Sam stops: I. If it misses, he throws again, and a second throw that goes in stops him: MI. After two misses he throws a third time, and that ends his turn either way: MMI or MMM. That is 4 ways. The idea to keep: in a tree diagram, stop a branch as soon as the rule says stop.
solutions.elegant: Each way is fixed by when the first ball goes in: on throw 1, throw 2, throw 3, or never. That is 4 ways. The idea to keep: sometimes you can count the stopping points instead of drawing every branch.

whyOnTest: A tree whose branches stop early tests whether students follow the stopping rule or just multiply by 2 for every throw.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
